summary: For ages 7–9, this topic secures naming and ordering the eight planets from the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), the fact that Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and one structural pattern: four small rocky inner planets then four large gas-giant outer planets. Pair a memorable mnemonic with a laid-out spatial model so order is both verbal and mapped, teach the inner/outer split as a 'noticing' children justify, and tell the Pluto story as science sharpening its definitions rather than a mistake. Keep scale honest but light, leaving full scale treatment to a dedicated later topic.
misconceptions: Pluto is still a planet / was 'demoted by mistake' (it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 when the definition of 'planet' was sharpened)
The planets are evenly spaced and similar in size (the outer giants are vastly bigger and the gaps grow enormously outward)
The order can start anywhere / Earth is first or in the middle (order is fixed FROM THE SUN: Mercury first, Earth third)
All planets are solid like Earth (the four outer giants are huge balls of gas/ice with no solid surface to stand on)
There are nine (or more) planets, or the Sun/Moon are planets (there are eight planets; the Sun is a star, the Moon orbits Earth)

activities.title: Walk the Sun-to-Neptune line
steps: Lay out (on a long paper strip, a hallway floor, or a laid-out line of cards) the eight planets starting at the Sun and moving outward.
Touch each planet in turn and say its name and its position number: Mercury (1), Venus (2), Earth (3), Mars (4), Jupiter (5), Saturn (6), Uranus (7), Neptune (8).
For each planet, say or place a label 'ROCKY' or 'GAS GIANT', and notice that the four near the Sun are small and solid while the four far out are enormous and gassy.
Learn and recite an order mnemonic (e.g. 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming') and then rebuild the line from memory.
Shade or mark a band around the inner four versus the outer four so the split is visible, and describe the widening gap between the rocky worlds and the giants.
activities.insight: The eight planets have a fixed order FROM THE SUN, and that order carries a real pattern — the four nearest are small and rocky, the four farthest are giants made mostly of gas (Uranus and Neptune also contain a lot of icy material) with no solid surface — not just a word-chain to memorise.

activities.title: Rebuild the order and sort rocky vs gas giant
steps: From a shuffled set of planet names or cards, place them back into the correct sequence from the Sun, checking each against the ordered line.
Sort the same eight into two groups: 'small & rocky, close to the Sun' versus 'giant & gassy, far out', and say why each belongs.
Add an 'is Pluto a planet?' decision: place Pluto into a separate 'dwarf planet' category and explain the choice.
Do repeated rounds of ordering until the sequence can be rebuilt confidently without the model.
activities.insight: Secure, independent recall of the planet order and confident classification of each planet as rocky inner or gas-giant outer, with Pluto correctly set aside as a dwarf planet.

activities.title: The Pluto story: when scientists sharpened the rule
steps: Discuss or read the short Pluto story: Pluto was once called the ninth planet; in 2006 scientists made the definition of 'planet' clearer and reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet.
Answer the diagnostic question: 'Pluto isn't one of the eight anymore. Did Pluto get destroyed, or fly away, or did something else happen? Tell me WHY it's no longer on the list.'
Explain in your own words that Pluto is still out there orbiting the Sun, exactly as before — only the naming rule changed.
Explore the follow-up: could there be other dwarf planets besides Pluto? (e.g. Ceres, Eris) and why scientists keep finding more.
activities.insight: Science updates its categories when definitions are sharpened. Pluto's change was a change of classification, not a physical event — Pluto is still orbiting the Sun.

checkQuestion: Put the planets in order from the Sun as best you can. Now — Pluto used to be called the ninth planet, but it isn't one of the eight anymore. Did Pluto get destroyed, or fly away, or did something else happen? Tell me WHY it's no longer on the list.
checkAnswer: The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Pluto was not destroyed and did not fly away — it is still out there orbiting the Sun. In 2006 scientists changed the DEFINITION of a planet and reclassified Pluto as a 'dwarf planet' because it is very small and shares its region of space with many other similar icy bodies. The four inner planets (Mercury–Mars) are small and rocky; the four outer ones (Jupiter–Neptune) are large gas giants.
